sentences.text: Eosphorosuchus possessed a notably short snout that would have enabled a powerful bite.
Its skull was both short and robust, standing taller relative to its length than those of Dibothrosuchus and Terrestrisuchus.
The antorbital fenestra – the opening in front of the eye socket – was almost completely closed, a condition that likely added strength to the skull.
Large, circular eye sockets and sharply curved, recurved teeth characterize the facial region.
Three osteoderms – bony plates in the skin – were broader, more circular, and bore a central keel compared with those of its close relatives.
A toe bone shows a healed swelling, indicating the animal survived a bite to its foot.
The remains of Eosphorosuchus were uncovered at the Coelophysis Quarry in Ghost Ranch, New Mexico.
A block containing the specimen was collected in 1948 by a team from the American Museum of Natural History.
The short, reinforced snout and recurved teeth suggest a predatory diet focused on other vertebrates.
Healed injuries on the foot demonstrate that individuals could survive serious wounds, indicating a capacity for recovery.
Eosphorosuchus is placed within Crocodylomorpha as an early member of the group.
The animal lived during the Late Triassic Rhaetian age.
Its fossils come from the Chinle Formation of Ghost Ranch, New Mexico.
Some researchers propose that the co-occurrence of Eosphorosuchus and Hesperosuchus in a mass-death assemblage indicates they divided terrestrial carnivorous niches.
